extracted.intended_audience: citizens, political reformers, and framers of constitutions; readers interested in principles for designing republican government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical provisions for designing constitutions and organizing governments so as to secure liberty, limit corruption, and promote the public good. Includes institutional design (representation, executive, legislature, judiciary), fiscal limits, oaths, and amendment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation's right to establish a constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing is, that a nation has a right to establish a constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitution is a rule for the conduct of government; a nation exercising this right will do so according to its judgment and may correct errors over time. The existence of this right underpins all subsequent design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution must be revisable/amendable
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the greatest improvements ... is the provision which the new constitutions make for occasionally revising, altering, and amending them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should not bind posterity forever; they must include explicit modes for revision to adapt to changing circumstances and prevent accumulated inconsistencies that provoke revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ends of government: general happiness, security, least expense
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming a constitution, it is first necessary to consider what are the ends for which government is necessary? Secondly, what are the best means, and the least expensive, for accomplishing those ends? ... The object of this association is the good of all, as well individually as collectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All constitutional design should be judged by whether it secures individuals’ peaceful pursuit of occupation, enjoyment of property, and minimizes public expense. Policy choices should be evaluated against these ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental powers: legislating and executing
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything appertaining to civil government, classes itself under one or other of these two divisions: that of legislating or enacting laws, and that of executing or administering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat judiciary as part of execution in functional terms; clearly define and separate the law-making function from law-execution to avoid confusion of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign authority is legislative; executive is subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign authority in any country is the power of making laws, and everything else is an official department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutions so the legislative power remains the supreme political authority; avoid allowing 'executive' offices to claim sovereign prerogatives beyond implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of extraordinary power in any individual
rubrics_metrics.description: No extraordinary power, capable of producing [disorder], should be lodged in the hands of any individual. The death, sickness, absence or defection, of any one individual in a government, ought to be a matter of no more consequence ... than if the same circumstance had taken place in a member of the English Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must be resilient to loss or incapacity of any person; avoid personal prerogatives that can paralyze or corrupt government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hereditary government; prefer representative government
rubrics_metrics.description: All hereditary government over a people is to them a species of slavery, and representative government is freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional arrangements should exclude hereditary rule and ensure representation; hereditary claims concentrate privilege and inhibit accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public remuneration: no extraordinary pay; offices paid only for service value
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no appropriations of public money to any person, beyond what his services in a state may be worth. ... the routine of office ... can never exceed the value of ten thousand pounds a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set reasonable, limited official salaries to prevent luxurious dependency and corruption; prohibit vast personal emoluments funded by public taxes. (Paine gives 'ten thousand pounds a year' as an upper benchmark.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality in provision across branches to avoid corrupting imbalance
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation can have no right to the time and services of any person at his own expense, whom it may choose to employ ... If the members of the legislature ... are to serve at their own expense that which is called the executive ... ought to serve in like manner. It is inconsistent to pay the one, and accept the service of the other gratis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide equitable support/compensation across government departments; paying one branch extravagantly while leaving another unpaid creates corruption and dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive office design: term limits, eligibility, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The president of the United States ... is elected only for four years. He is not only responsible in the general sense ... he cannot be elected under thirty-five years of age; and he must be a native of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement limited terms, age/nativity or other eligibility requirements, and specific accountability (e.g., trial/impeachment mechanisms) for chief executives to constrain power and secure responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude foreigners from highest executive trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The presidency in America ... is the only office from which a foreigner is excluded, and in England it is the only one to which he is admitted. A foreigner cannot be a member of Parliament, but he may be what is called a king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disallow persons with foreign allegiance or ties from holding the most consequential executive offices; foreign incumbency concentrates risks of foreign influence and misalignment with national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish personal oaths; allegiance should be to the nation only
rubrics_metrics.description: Another reform ... is the exploding all oaths of personality. The oath of allegiance in America is to the nation only. ... The oath, called the civic oath, in France, 'the nation, the law, and the king,' is improper. All personal oaths ought to be abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths should bind officials to the nation (and law) rather than to persons or offices; personal oaths perpetuate fealty and slavery and invite misuse of religious formulae to endorse domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative composition: evaluate single vs two houses and avoid systemic inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections against two houses: minority may govern majority, possibility of inconsistency, arbitrary checks. Objection against a single house: committing too soon. Proposed improvement: one representation divided by lot into parts, successive debates without votes, then whole assembly votes; rotate one-third replacement yearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh trade-offs between bicameral and unicameral legislatures. Consider procedural devices (division by lot; staged debate; staggered renewal of representatives) to combine deliberation with renewal and avoid both premature commitments and deadlocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer principles to blind reliance on precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Government by precedent, without any regard to the principle of the precedent, is one of the vilest systems ... precedents ought to operate as a warning, and not as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess law and policy against underlying principles rather than treating ancient precedents as authoritative per se; avoid 'political popery' that uses reverence for antiquity to suppress reflection and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be practicable to execute
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws difficult to be executed cannot be generally good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer legislation that can realistically be administered; administrative feasibility is a criterion of lawfulness and prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution should restrain taxation and limit public expense
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill of rights ... has undoubtedly been the most productive machine of taxation that was ever invented. ... In forming a constitution ... what are the best means, and the least expensive, for accomplishing those ends?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design fiscal constraints into constitutional structure to prevent excessive taxation, especially to fund foreign wars or court extravagance; keep public expense aligned with the real needs of civil government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote commerce as a means of civilisation and peace
rubrics_metrics.description: If commerce were permitted to act to the universal extent it is capable, it would extirpate the system of war ... Commerce is a pacific system, operating to cordialise mankind, by rendering nations ... useful to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage policies that facilitate free commercial intercourse between peoples to reduce incentives for war, spread prosperity, and broaden the base of civilization that restrains despotic government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncivilized foreign policy that perpetuates wars and drains the public
rubrics_metrics.description: All the European governments ... are constructed not on the principle of universal civilisation, but on the reverse of it ... governments being yet in an uncivilised state, and almost continually at war, they pervert the abundance which civilised life produces to carry on the uncivilised part to a greater extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame foreign-policy and defense arrangements so they do not institutionalize perpetual war as a revenue source; reduce external pretences for taxation and the pretexts that prop up court governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure continuity of government through representation and staggered renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: All the constitutions of America are on a plan that excludes the childish embarrassments which occur in monarchical countries. ... The system of representation provides for everything, and is the only system in which nations and governments can always appear in their proper character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build representative mechanisms (e.g., staggered terms, replacements by election) so that government never halts for want of a single individual and remains resilient to vacancies or incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent patronage and corruption by removing extraordinary perquisites
rubrics_metrics.description: When once such a vicious system is established [extraordinary pay & power] it becomes the guard and protection of all inferior abuses. The man who is in the receipt of a million a year is the last person to promote a spirit of reform ... It is made up of a band of parasites, living in luxurious indolence, out of the public taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design appointment, remuneration, and place-creation powers to minimize opportunities for clientelism; limit executive authority to create patronage that entrenches abuses.
